claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by distinct motor phenomena that are expressed asynchronously.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by distinct motor phenomena that are expressed asynchronously.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that establishes the nature of PD motor symptoms.

claim: Support vector regression analysis of microelectrode and electrocorticography recordings revealed that tremor and bradykinesia had nearly opposite neural signatures.
source: Support vector regression analysis of microelectrode and electrocorticography recordings revealed that tremor and bradykinesia had nearly opposite neural signatures, while effective motor control displayed unique, differentiating features.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of neural recordings.

claim: Effective motor control displayed unique, differentiating features from tremor and bradykinesia.
source: Support vector regression analysis of microelectrode and electrocorticography recordings revealed that tremor and bradykinesia had nearly opposite neural signatures, while effective motor control displayed unique, differentiating features.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of neural recordings.

claim: Cortical decoding generally outperformed subcortical decoding.
source: Cortical decoding generally outperformed subcortical decoding.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a comparative finding from the study.

claim: Within the subthalamic nucleus (STN), tremor and bradykinesia were better decoded from distinct subregions.
source: Within the subthalamic nucleus (STN), tremor and bradykinesia were better decoded from distinct subregions.
evidence: This is a primary finding regarding anatomical localization within the STN.

claim: Parkinson's disease is a common and complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the dynamic expression of particular motor features such as tremor and bradykinesia.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common and complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the dynamic expression of particular motor features such as tremor and bradykinesia (Armstrong and Okun, 2020; Parkinson, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Distinct motor signs of PD are expressed variably across patients and may respond differently to dopamine replacement therapy.
source: These distinct motor signs are expressed variably across patients and may respond differently to dopamine replacement therapy; their differential expression is often used to classify patients into phenotypic subtypes (Koller, 1986; Sethi, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both tremor-dominant and non-tremor-dominant patient subtypes respond to high-frequency deep brain stimulation (DBS) applied to the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
source: Despite this heterogeneity, both of these motor features (and both tremor-dominant and non-tremor-dominant patient subtypes) respond to high-frequency deep brain stimulation (DBS) applied to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) (Katz et al., 2015; Limousin et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Closed-loop DBS has shown promising therapeutic potential primarily toward alleviating bradykinesia.
source: DBS delivered in a closed-loop fashion (i.e., in response to neurophysiological biomarkers) has shown promising therapeutic potential primarily toward alleviating bradykinesia (Little et al., 2016a; Little et al., 2016b), but current efforts focusing on β frequency oscillations (15–30 Hz) have been shown to inadequately treat or worsen tremor in some cases (Piña-Fuentes et al., 2020; Velisar et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Current closed-loop DBS efforts focusing on β frequency oscillations (15–30 Hz) have been shown to inadequately treat or worsen tremor in some cases.
source: DBS delivered in a closed-loop fashion (i.e., in response to neurophysiological biomarkers) has shown promising therapeutic potential primarily toward alleviating bradykinesia (Little et al., 2016a; Little et al., 2016b), but current efforts focusing on β frequency oscillations (15–30 Hz) have been shown to inadequately treat or worsen tremor in some cases (Piña-Fuentes et al., 2020; Velisar et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: STN LFP recordings from patients with different PD subtypes have revealed distinct patterns of oscillatory activity.
source: To this point, STN LFP recordings from patients with different PD subtypes have revealed distinct patterns of oscillatory activity (Telkes et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Specific stimulation sites within the STN have been associated with the preferential reduction of individual motor signs.
source: In addition to spectral variability, specific stimulation sites within the STN have been associated with the preferential reduction of individual motor signs (Akram et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: STN sites associated with preferential reduction of individual motor signs were associated with specific patterns of anatomical connectivity with cortical structures.
source: Moreover, these STN sites were associated with specific patterns of anatomical connectivity with cortical structures (Haynes and Haber, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Overlapping subdivisions of basal-ganglia-cortical circuits have been found to encode separate aspects of movement.
source: Much like how overlapping subdivisions of basal-ganglia-cortical circuits have been found to encode separate aspects of movement (Mosher et al., 2021; Neumann et al., 2018), separate motor features may be mediated by different sub-circuits involving the STN and sensorimotor cortex (Gibson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Separate motor features may be mediated by different sub-circuits involving the STN and sensorimotor cortex.
source: Much like how overlapping subdivisions of basal-ganglia-cortical circuits have been found to encode separate aspects of movement (Mosher et al., 2021; Neumann et al., 2018), separate motor features may be mediated by different sub-circuits involving the STN and sensorimotor cortex (Gibson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Twenty-seven patients with PD undergoing STN DBS implantation and 17 age-matched controls performed a visual-motor task.
source: Twenty-seven patients with PD undergoing STN DBS implantation and 17 age-matched controls performed a visual-motor task in which they followed an on-screen target with a cursor controlled by either a joystick or a stylus and tablet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the study design and participant numbers.

claim: PD patients demonstrated increased tremor compared to control subjects.
source: The resulting metric distributions for PD vs. control subjects demonstrated increased tremor for PD patients (n=6498 epochs across 44 subjects, PD vs. control, LMM coefficient/LMM β=0.337, Z=2.169, p=0.030), but only a trend for decreased speed (PD vs. control, LMM β=−0.592, Z=−1.194, p=0.232) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: PD patients showed only a trend for decreased speed compared to control subjects in the fixed-pattern task.
source: The resulting metric distributions for PD vs. control subjects demonstrated increased tremor for PD patients (n=6498 epochs across 44 subjects, PD vs. control, LMM coefficient/LMM β=0.337, Z=2.169, p=0.030), but only a trend for decreased speed (PD vs. control, LMM β=−0.592, Z=−1.194, p=0.232) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: In the random-pattern version of the task, the PD cursor speed distribution was shifted to the left (i.e., slower) relative to control subjects.
source: Nonetheless, in the random-pattern version, the PD cursor speed distribution was shifted to the left (i.e., slower) relative to control subjects (n=1123 epochs across 9 subjects, PD vs. control, LMM β=−1.004, Z=−2.210, p=0.027).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Tremor amplitude positively correlated with the UPDRS resting tremor subscore.
source: Indeed, tremor amplitude positively correlated with the resting tremor subscore (ρ=0.607, p=0.001, n=24 PD subjects, Spearman correlation) (Figure 1D) and slowness positively correlated with the hand open/close subscore (a subscore used in part to assess bradykinesia) (ρ=0.406, p=0.035, Spearman correlation) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation finding from the study data.

claim: Slowness positively correlated with the UPDRS hand open/close subscore.
source: Indeed, tremor amplitude positively correlated with the resting tremor subscore (ρ=0.607, p=0.001, n=24 PD subjects, Spearman correlation) (Figure 1D) and slowness positively correlated with the hand open/close subscore (a subscore used in part to assess bradykinesia) (ρ=0.406, p=0.035, Spearman correlation) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation finding from the study data.

claim: Tremor and slowness were inversely expressed in time.
source: Relative to each other, tremor and slowness typically did not co-occur but rather were inversely expressed in time (n=27 subjects, tremor × slowness, LMM β=−0.584, Z=−19.351, p=2.00*10–83) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Tremor was typically expressed continuously for longer periods (autocorrelogram full-width half-maximum [FWHM], 0.898 s) as opposed to slowness (0.297 s).
source: Here, tremor was typically expressed continuously for longer periods (autocorrelogram full-width half-maximum [FWHM], 0.898 s) as opposed to slowness (0.297 s) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The median duration of symptomatic tremor episodes was 2.000 s, and slowness episodes lasted for 0.500 s.
source: The median duration of symptomatic tremor episodes was 2.000 s, and slowness episodes lasted for 0.500 s (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Effective motor control was expressed on longer timescales (FWHM = 3.784 s, median state length = 7.900 s) compared to tremor and slowness.
source: Compared to other metrics, effective motor control was expressed on longer timescales (FWHM = 3.784 s, median state length = 7.900 s) (Figure 2A, C and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: A total of 203 microelectrode and 176 macroelectrode recordings were acquired from the STN as patients performed the task.
source: A total of 203 microelectrode and 176 macroelectrode recordings (microelectrode tips and macroelectrode contacts separated by 3 mm on the same electrodes) were acquired from the STN as patients performed the task.
evidence: This describes the data collection in the study.

claim: Microelectrode tremor decoding models positively weighted low-frequency features (θ,α,β; 4–21 Hz).
source: Microelectrode tremor decoding models positively weighted low-frequency features (θ,α,β; 4–21 Hz; p<0.001, permutation test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Microelectrode tremor decoding models positively weighted hfo (275–375 Hz) frequencies.
source: Hfo (275–375 Hz) weights were also positively associated with tremor decoding (p<0.014, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Macroelectrode tremor decoding models negatively weighed β power (14–41 Hz) while positively weighing γ/hfo activity (60–375 Hz).
source: In contrast, macroelectrode tremor decoding models negatively weighed β power (14–41 Hz; p<0.026, permutation test) while positively weighing γ/hfo activity (60–375 Hz; p<0.011, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Macroelectrode slowness decoding models positively weighted β frequencies (12–30 Hz) along with negative γ/hfo weights (33–375 Hz).
source: Macroelectrode decoding models positively weighted β frequencies (12–30 Hz; p<0.006, permutation test) along with negative γ/hfo weights (33–375 Hz; p<0.001, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Hfo frequencies (225–375 Hz) were elevated during tremor in both micro/macroelectrode recordings when comparing tremor and slowness model features directly.
source: Tremor and slowness model features differed when compared directly, with hfo frequencies (225–375 Hz) being elevated during tremor in both micro/macroelectrode recordings (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of SVR model feature weights.

claim: When directly comparing tremor and slowness decoding performance on tremor-trained models, slowness decoding was inferior for both microelectrode and macroelectrode recordings.
source: When directly comparing tremor and slowness decoding performance on tremor-trained models, slowness decoding was inferior for both microelectrode (tremor v. slowness decoding, r2=0.232±0.197 v. 0.002±0.001; LMM β=0.101, Z=11.242, p=2.54*10–29) and macroelectrode (tremor v. slowness decoding, r2=0.205±0.172 v. 0.002±0.001; LMM β=0.086, Z=10.294, p=7.53*10–25) recordings.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from cross-metric decoding analysis.

claim: Individual tremor expression positively correlated with tremor decoding performance.
source: Here, we found that task-based tremor distribution medians positively correlated with individual's highest decoding performance (n=24 patients, ρ=0.442, p=0.031).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation finding from the study data.

claim: Effective motor control decoding was characterized by the absence of β (10–28 Hz) power in both micro- and macroelectrode recordings.
source: Effective motor control decoding was characterized by the absence of β (10–28 Hz) power in both micro- and macroelectrode recordings (p<0.006, permutation test), while macroelectrodes also exhibited positive γ power weights (30–175 Hz; p<0.020, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Macroelectrode effective motor control decoding exhibited positive γ power weights (30–175 Hz).
source: Effective motor control decoding was characterized by the absence of β (10–28 Hz) power in both micro- and macroelectrode recordings (p<0.006, permutation test), while macroelectrodes also exhibited positive γ power weights (30–175 Hz; p<0.020, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVR model feature weights.

claim: Full-spectrum decoding had significantly greater performance than beta-only decoding for macroelectrode recordings for all three metrics.
source: Full-spectrum decoding had significantly greater performance for macroelectrode (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.018–0.035, Z=2.388–3.949, p<0.017) and microelectrode (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.014–0.017, Z=2.241–3.154, p<0.025) for all three metrics, with the exception of microelectrode-tremor decoding (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.014, Z=1.548, p=0.122).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing different decoding approaches.

claim: Full-spectrum decoding had significantly greater performance than beta-only decoding for microelectrode recordings for slowness and effective motor control, but not for tremor.
source: Full-spectrum decoding had significantly greater performance for macroelectrode (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.018–0.035, Z=2.388–3.949, p<0.017) and microelectrode (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.014–0.017, Z=2.241–3.154, p<0.025) for all three metrics, with the exception of microelectrode-tremor decoding (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.014, Z=1.548, p=0.122).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing different decoding approaches.

claim: Tremor was better decoded in recordings from dorsolateral STN (x=-14.0,y=-13.0,z=-5.0; Z=2.116,p=0.017).
source: Tremor was better decoded in recordings from dorsolateral STN (n=182 MER sites, x=-14.0,y=-13.0,z=-5.0; Z=2.116,p=0.017), whereas slowness was better decoded from recordings in central/ventromedial STN (x=-12.0,y=-14.0,z=-6.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from the imaging-based reconstruction.

claim: Slowness was better decoded from recordings in central/ventromedial STN (x=-12.0,y=-14.0,z=-6.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028).
source: Tremor was better decoded in recordings from dorsolateral STN (n=182 MER sites, x=-14.0,y=-13.0,z=-5.0; Z=2.116,p=0.017), whereas slowness was better decoded from recordings in central/ventromedial STN (x=-12.0,y=-14.0,z=-6.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from the imaging-based reconstruction.

claim: In high-density STN survey recordings, tremor was optimally decoded at (x=−13.0,y=−13.0,z=−5.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028).
source: Across these recordings, tremor was optimally decoded at (x=−13.0,y=−13.0,z=−5.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028), while slowness was optimally decoded at (x=−12.0,y=−15.0,z=−8.0; Z=1.937,p=0.026).
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from the high-density STN survey.

claim: In high-density STN survey recordings, slowness was optimally decoded at (x=−12.0,y=−15.0,z=−8.0; Z=1.937,p=0.026).
source: Across these recordings, tremor was optimally decoded at (x=−13.0,y=−13.0,z=−5.0; Z=1.911,p=0.028), while slowness was optimally decoded at (x=−12.0,y=−15.0,z=−8.0; Z=1.937,p=0.026).
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from the high-density STN survey.

claim: Ten subjects had ECoG recordings from sensorimotor cortex (motor cortex: n=16 contacts, somatosensory cortex: n=15).
source: Ten subjects additionally had ECoG recordings from sensorimotor cortex (motor cortex: n=16 contacts, somatosensory cortex: n=15, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data collection in the study.

claim: Cortical tremor models had positive weights associated with θ frequencies (5–7 Hz).
source: Tremor models additionally had positive weights associated with θ frequencies (5–7 Hz, p=0.003, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of cortical SVR model feature weights.

claim: ECoG full-spectrum decoding was superior to beta-only decoding for tremor and effective motor control, but equivalent for slowness.
source: And similarly to STN recordings, ECoG full-spectrum decoding was superior for tremor and effective motor control (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=0.017–0.024, Z=2.224–2.577, p<0.026), but equivalent for slowness (full vs. beta-only decoding, LMM β=−0.013, Z=−1.531, p=0.126).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing different decoding approaches.

claim: Slowness decoding had peaks in medial motor (x=-37.5,y=-15.8,z=+70.2; T=2.210, p=0.030) and somatosensory (x=-34.4,y=-37.4,z=+71.0; T=2.340,p=0.022) cortices.
source: Comparing tremor and slowness decoding performance by cortical anatomy revealed that slowness decoding had peaks in medial motor (n=31 ECoG recording sites, x=-37.5,y=-15.8,z=+70.2; T=2.210, p=0.030) and somatosensory (x=-34.4,y=-37.4,z=+71.0; T=2.340,p=0.022) cortices.
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from cortical recordings.

claim: A trending tremor decoding peak was observed in lateral somatosensory cortex (x=-50.2,y=-31.8,z=+64.0; T=1.700,p=0.093).
source: We also observed a trending tremor decoding peak in lateral somatosensory cortex (x=-50.2,y=-31.8,z=+64.0; T=1.700,p=0.093) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a spatial analysis finding from cortical recordings.

claim: ECoG tremor decoding models exhibited higher performance than micro-STN recordings.
source: ECoG tremor decoding models exhibited higher performance than micro-STN recordings (ECoG v. micro-STN, r2=0.323±0.153 v. 0.240±0.200, LMM β=0.047, Z=2.504, p=0.012), but only trended higher relative to macro-STN recordings (ECoG v. macro-STN, r2=0.323±0.153 v. 0.294±0.222, LMM β=0.019, Z=1.001, p=0.317).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing decoding performance across recording types.

claim: ECoG slowness decoding performance was higher than both macro-STN and micro-STN recordings.
source: Slowness decoding performance on the other hand was higher in ECoG models relative to both macro-STN (ECoG v. macro-STN, r2=0.314±0.143 v. 0.195±0.105, LMM β=0.061, Z=4.445, p=8.78*10–6) and micro-STN (ECoG v. micro-STN, r2=0.314±0.143 v. 0.128±0.134, LMM β=0.096, Z=7.025, p=2.14*10–12) recordings.
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing decoding performance across recording types.

claim: ECoG effective motor control decoding models exhibited superior decoding performance to micro-STN but not macro-STN recordings.
source: Like tremor, effective motor control ECoG decoding models exhibited superior decoding performance to micro-STN (ECoG v. micro-STN, r2=0.233±0.105 v. 0.133±0.096, LMM β=−0.038, Z=−3.140, p=0.002), but not macro-STN (ECoG v. macro-STN, r2=0.233±0.105 v. 0.219±0.098, LMM β=0.004, Z=0.312, p=0.755) recordings.
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing decoding performance across recording types.

claim: Local decoding models outperformed pairwise cortical-subthalamic decoding models across all metrics.
source: Across all metrics, local decoding models outperformed pairwise decoding models (tremor: ECoG v. EcoG/macro-STN, r2=0.323±0.153 v. 0.075±0.029, LMM β=0.133, Z=15.073, p=2.43*10–51; slowness: ECoG v. EcoG/macro-STN, r2=0.314±0.143 v. 0.098±0.057, LMM β=0.123, Z=14.420, p=3.89*10–47; effective motor control: ECoG v. EcoG/macro-STN, r2=0.233±0.105 v. 0.096±0.050, LMM β=0.065, Z=10.213, p=1.73*10–24).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing local versus pairwise decoding approaches.

claim: Slowness coherence models positively weighed frequencies within the β range (12–26 Hz) when compared to tremor and effective motor control decoding models.
source: When examining decoding coherence features, slowness models positively weighed frequencies within the β range (12–26 Hz, p<0.0005, permutation test) when compared to tremor and effective motor control decoding models.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of coherence-based decoding model features.

claim: In the STN, tremor was characterized by lower-frequency (θ,α) oscillations in microelectrodes, whereas slowness was characterized by the presence of β oscillations and the absence of γ oscillations in macroelectrodes.
source: In the STN, tremor was characterized by lower-frequency (θ,α) oscillations in microelectrodes, whereas slowness was characterized by the presence of β oscillations and the absence of γ oscillations in macroelectrodes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from the neural decoding analysis.

claim: Some frequency bands in isolation (θ,β) have been found to correlate with clinical measures of tremor and bradykinesia.
source: Some of these frequency bands in isolation (θ,β) have been found to correlate with clinical measures of tremor and bradykinesia (Asch et al., 2020; Neumann et al., 2016; Nie et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Optimal tremor decoding may have included activity from zona incerta, a stimulation site commonly thought to be critical for alleviating tremor.
source: Optimal tremor decoding may have included activity from zona incerta, a stimulation site commonly thought to be critical for alleviating tremor (Plaha et al., 2008; Reck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Optimal stimulation sites to alleviate tremor and bradykinesia correspond to the dorsolateral-tremor/ventromedial-slowness topography found in this study.
source: Indeed, optimal stimulation sites to alleviate tremor and bradykinesia correspond to our dorsolateral-tremor/ventromedial-slowness topography (Akram et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement connects the study findings to prior literature via citation.

claim: Several groups have localized β frequency activity to dorsolateral STN, observed to be located inferiorly to tremor-related higher frequency oscillations.
source: While several groups have localized β frequency activity to dorsolateral STN, this has been observed to be located inferiorly to tremor-related higher frequency oscillations (Tamir et al., 2020; Telkes et al., 2018; van Wijk et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In macaques, motor cortex projects to the dorsal portion of the STN, and the ventral STN receives projections from prefrontal cortex.
source: In macaques, motor cortex projects to the dorsal portion of the STN, and the ventral STN receives projections from prefrontal cortex (Haynes and Haber, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In both macaques and humans, the ventral STN has been associated with stopping movement, while the dorsal STN is more associated with motor initiation and selection.
source: In both macaques and humans, the ventral STN has been associated with stopping movement, while the dorsal STN is more associated with motor initiation and selection (Chen et al., 2020; Mosher et al., 2021; Pasquereau and Turner, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The co-occurrence of tremor-frequency (4–8 Hz; θ) activity in both STN and cortical recordings is consistent with previous work finding tremor-frequency oscillations (θ) originating in the STN and propagating/synchronizing to motor cortex during tremor.
source: In addition, the co-occurrence of tremor-frequency (4–8 Hz; θ) activity in both STN and cortical recordings is consistent with previous work finding tremor-frequency oscillations (θ) originating in the STN and propagating/synchronizing to motor cortex during tremor (Hirschmann et al., 2013; Lauro et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement connects the study findings to prior literature via citations.

claim: Cortical recordings were generally superior to STN-based decoding as previously reported.
source: In general, cortical recordings were equally capable of decoding tremor or slowness and were generally superior to STN-based decoding as previously reported (Merk et al., 2022b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies have shown that tremor decreases β oscillations across cortex.
source: As previous studies have shown that tremor decreases β oscillations across cortex (Qasim et al., 2016), and others have shown increased narrowband γ activity during hyperkinetic/dyskinetic states (Swann et al., 2016), here we demonstrate a 'push-pull' relationship between these frequency bands in the alternating expression of tremor and slowness, and when comparing slowness and effective motor control models.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Others have shown increased narrowband γ activity during hyperkinetic/dyskinetic states.
source: As previous studies have shown that tremor decreases β oscillations across cortex (Qasim et al., 2016), and others have shown increased narrowband γ activity during hyperkinetic/dyskinetic states (Swann et al., 2016), here we demonstrate a 'push-pull' relationship between these frequency bands in the alternating expression of tremor and slowness, and when comparing slowness and effective motor control models.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Current closed-loop DBS paradigms trigger stimulation based on one or two frequency bands representing PD symptoms.
source: While current closed-loop DBS paradigms trigger stimulation based on one or two frequency bands representing PD symptoms (Kehnemouyi et al., 2021), our results argue for the potential utility of a more targeted neurophysiological approach to PD state identification: more dorsal STN contacts may better sense signals reflecting tremor, while more ventral STN contacts may better identify signals corresponding to bradykinesia.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: More dorsal STN contacts may better sense signals reflecting tremor, while more ventral STN contacts may better identify signals corresponding to bradykinesia.
source: While current closed-loop DBS paradigms trigger stimulation based on one or two frequency bands representing PD symptoms (Kehnemouyi et al., 2021), our results argue for the potential utility of a more targeted neurophysiological approach to PD state identification: more dorsal STN contacts may better sense signals reflecting tremor, while more ventral STN contacts may better identify signals corresponding to bradykinesia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study findings about potential clinical applications.

claim: Future neuromodulation paradigms could be derived not simply to disrupt pathological activity but actually to sustain the neurophysiological γ frequency 'targets' of effective motor control.
source: Most importantly, future neuromodulation paradigms could be derived not simply to disrupt pathological activity but actually to sustain the neurophysiological γ frequency 'targets' of effective motor control.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications based on the study findings.

claim: Chronic cortical recordings could work in concert with STN recordings to help identify precise motor states associated with specific aspects of disease expression.
source: Looking ahead, chronic cortical recordings could work in concert with STN recordings to help identify precise motor states associated with specific aspects of disease expression much like prior work with essential tremor (He et al., 2021; Opri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other studies decoding PD motor dysfunction from STN recordings have investigated the use of several decoding techniques (hidden Markov models, logistic regression, Kalman filters).
source: While other studies decoding PD motor dysfunction from STN recordings have investigated the use of several decoding techniques (hidden Markov models, logistic regression, Kalman filters), their complexity/computational requirements will require balancing potential therapeutic benefits with the computational/power limitations of implanted pulse generators (Hirschmann et al., 2017; Merk et al., 2022a; Shah et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The complexity/computational requirements of advanced decoding techniques will require balancing potential therapeutic benefits with the computational/power limitations of implanted pulse generators.
source: While other studies decoding PD motor dysfunction from STN recordings have investigated the use of several decoding techniques (hidden Markov models, logistic regression, Kalman filters), their complexity/computational requirements will require balancing potential therapeutic benefits with the computational/power limitations of implanted pulse generators (Hirschmann et al., 2017; Merk et al., 2022a; Shah et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about practical considerations for clinical implementation.

claim: The linear SVR approach was robustly able to fit patient- and symptom-specific decoding models in an interpretable and iterable fashion.
source: Although relatively simple, our linear SVR approach was robustly able to fit patient- and symptom-specific decoding models in an interpretable and iterable fashion.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's methodological approach and its performance.

claim: Patients were withdrawn from dopaminergic medication for at least 12 hr prior to surgery.
source: Further, because patients were withdrawn from dopaminergic medication for at least 12 hr prior to surgery, exacerbated patient symptoms in the operating room may produce improved model decoding performance relative to models trained on patients taking dopaminergic medication in the natural setting.
evidence: This describes a methodological aspect of the study.

claim: 32 subjects (n=27 subjects in stationary-recording experiments, n=5 subjects in high-density recording experiments) underwent STN DBS.
source: In this report, 32 subjects (n=27 subjects in stationary-recording experiments, n=5 subjects in high-density recording experiments) (4F, 28M; aged 47.5–78.5 years) underwent STN DBS.

claim: There was no significant age difference between patient and control subjects (patient v. control subjects ages, 65.2±7.9 vs 63.2±9.3, Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.450).
source: Controls were required simply to be free of any diagnosed or suspected movement disorder and to have no physical limitation preventing them from seeing the display or using the manipulandum. There was a strong male bias in the patient population (2F, 25M) and a female preponderance in the control population (14F, 3M), reflecting weaker overall biases in the prevalence of PD and the clinical utilization of DBS therapy (Accolla et al., 2007; Hariz et al., 2011; Rumalla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of demographic characteristics.
